flawed_step: The assertion that planarity guarantees a single Kempe-chain interchange eliminating one color from N(v) is false.
counterexample: Let V(G)={v,x1,x2,x3,x4,x5}. Add all edges vxi; the cycle edges x1x2,x2x3,x3x4,x4x5,x5x1; and chords x2x4,x2x5. This is planar: draw the 5-cycle with v and its spokes inside, and the two noncrossing chords outside. Color G-v by c(x1)=c(x3)=1, c(x2)=2, c(x4)=3, c(x5)=4. This is proper, and all four colors occur on N(v). The bichromatic components meeting N(v) are: for {1,2}, {x1,x2,x3}; for {1,3}, {x1} and {x3,x4}; for {1,4}, {x1,x5} and {x3}; for {2,3}, {x2,x4}; for {2,4}, {x2,x5}; and for {3,4}, {x4,x5}. Swapping the {1,2} component preserves both colors by exchanging color 2 with the two color-1 vertices. For {1,3} or {1,4}, either component swap leaves the other color-1 vertex and also leaves or creates both colors in the pair. For each pair among {2,3,4}, its two uniquely colored neighbors lie in the same component, so swapping merely exchanges their colors. Hence every single interchange leaves all four colors on N(v).
assessment_summary: This explicit six-vertex planar graph satisfies every hypothesis, but no single Kempe-chain interchange reduces the number of colors on the five neighbors of v.
